entry.article_text: It’s a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years.Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday devoted a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.Trump headlined a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state.Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday.The president noted to the crowd that he had flown eight hours to rally for Sullivan, whom he called “one of the best and most respected senators in D.C.” Sullivan, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who is running to put “Alaska first” and emphasizing cost-of-living issues.During Tuesday's rally, Trump announced that Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project that he has been highlighting amid Sullivan's campaign and that it would invest more than $4 billion. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. The White House did not immediately provide further details.Trump also said the Federal Communications Commission would vote in the coming weeks on investing an additional $162 million in expanding high-speed internet access in Alaska. And he announced pardons for two men who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations for tampering with federally mandated monitoring devices on certain vehicles.Trump and Vance have been trying to boost Sullivan repeatedlyDemocrats last won a Senate seat in Alaska in 2008, and the state hasn’t elected a governor from that party since 1998. The only time Alaska didn’t vote Republican for president was during Lyndon B. Johnson’s landslide 1964 reelection.Yet high gasoline prices from the Iran war and persistently elevated inflation have damaged Trump’s approval ratings enough to leave Democrats dreaming of Alaska upsets.Alaska pollster Ivan Moore said he's seen a decline in Trump's support statewide that mirrors the president's falling approval ratings nationally. That means the Senate race may be decided by Trump 2024 voters who are now unsure they still back him.“The visit is certainly appropriate. Whether the visit will be effective or not is another matter," said Moore, who said when he first heard that Trump would visit Alaska, he didn't believe it would actually happen.The Trump administration has prioritized expanding oil and gas drilling in the state. Vice President JD Vance last week campaigned in Fairbanks for Sullivan and Republican Rep. Nick Begich.Sullivan recently joined Trump in the Oval Office, where the president announced a $54 billion investment by South Korea's government into the proposed Alaska gas project. That's despite South Korea saying the deal, and its total value, haven't been finalized.Versions of a gas project have been proposed in Alaska for decades.Trump trekking four time zones west to get to Sullivan’s home turf — an unusually long trip so close to the midterms — is his strongest show of support for the incumbent.Trump last campaigned in Alaska to try to defeat a fellow RepublicanAlaska is home to around 740,000 people, making it slightly less populous than Denver. It ranks 48th out of 50 states in population, smaller than all but Vermont and Wyoming.Trump nonetheless headlined a 2022 rally in Anchorage opposing Republican Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski after she voted to convict him on a charge of incitement of insurrection during his second impeachment trial, following the attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021.Trump endorsed Kelly Tshibaka, who challenged Murkowski that year, but that didn't stop incumbent Murkowski from winning reelection.In Wasilla, Max Christensen was waiting in line for the rally and said he hoped to hear more specifics from Trump about the natural gas project, and said he was “really curious just to see how he’s going to handle things like inflation and gas prices and things like that.”Christensen, 22, said he thinks Trump has been a great president “despite all his flaws and stuff," adding, “I think he really does genuinely care about the people of the United States of America.”This year, there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballotTrump has complained about Alaska’s unique elections system. The state has open primaries, in which the four top vote-getters — regardless of party affiliation — advance to the general election, which uses ranked choice voting.RELATED STORY | Republicans are flooding Senate races with ad money, but paying a premiumThat's led to a scenario where there also will be another Dan Sullivan on the November ballot: retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whom Trump and other allies of Sen. Sullivan have called a sham candidate. Sullivan has denied this, but Trump continued to hammer the other Sullivan at his rally.“They found a guy named Dan Sullivan, they put him up to get things a little confused,” Trump said, as he repeatedly urged his supporters to vote for “the real Dan Sullivan.”Trump also touted Begich, who is facing a competitive challenge from Bill Hill, an independent.Alaska has a history of rewarding candidates with an independent streak — something Vance acknowledged during his trip to Fairbanks last week."In very deep red years, Alaska is competitive. In very deep blue years, Alaska is still competitive,” Vance said. “I think it’s just a reality of the politics of the state.”Independence has been hard to find in the Republican Party, where Trump for years has had total control. Some Republicans facing tough elections have begun tiptoeing away from the president on key issues such as Iran and tariffs, but not Sullivan, who has been vocal in supporting both.Trump also questioned why three Republicans were running against a Democrat for governor and endorsed Bernadette Wilson, who finished third in the August primary but was the top vote-getting Republican. This came at the same time state GOP leaders — including outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy — are urging voters to rank Republicans on the ballot.Many Republicans — despite reservations with ranked voting — have seen a ranking strategy in that race as crucial for Republicans trying to win the seat.Trump's trade war with Canada may also be a factorTrump has also triggered a trade war with Canada, which shares a 1,500-plus-mile border with Alaska and is among the state's most important trading partners.The U.S. banned nearly $1 billion worth of imports from its neighbor — including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles — after previously imposing 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian products. Canada has responded with reciprocal bans and its own import levies, and the back-and-forth could raise prices for Alaska consumers.RELATED STORY | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsMaking Canada an enemy of sorts is "discomforting" for many Alaskans, said pollster Moore.“We associate, I think, probably more closely with the Canadians — more than a lot of the Lower 48," he said.

entry.title: Martin County approves emergency transit plan to restore MARTY bus service after abrupt shutdown
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners have approved emergency measures aimed at restoring MARTY bus service after an abrupt shutdown last week left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs. County leaders voted Tuesday to terminate their contract with Martin County Transit and begin negotiating an emergency one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county's transit system. WATCH: Martin County moves to restore MARTY buses Martin County moves to restore MARTY bus service The move comes as the county works to quickly restore public transportation service for residents who rely on MARTY buses to get to work, medical appointments and other essential destinations. County moves forward with emergency contract The emergency action follows last week's sudden shutdown of MARTY bus service, which county officials say disrupted transportation across the community. 'We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract,' said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton. The proposed agreement with MTM Transit would serve as a temporary solution while county leaders develop a longer-term plan for public transportation service. County officials say restoring service is a top priority. 'The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back,' Gorton said. Drivers hope to return to work The shutdown has created uncertainty for employees who suddenly found themselves without work. 'It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating,' said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. entry.title: Van driver sought after fleeing fatal crash involving scooter in Fort Pierce - WPBF
entry.summary: Van driver sought after fleeing fatal crash involving scooter in Fort Pierce    WPBF
entry.article_text: Police are searching for a hit-and-run cargo van driver accused of fatally striking a 44-year-old man riding a gas scooter before he crashed into a nearby business and ran away in Fort Pierce. On Tuesday, the victim was identified as Andy Ramon Martinez-Pantoja. Police officers received multiple 911 calls just before 9 p.m. Sunday about a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle, which later was identified as a gas scooter, close to the intersection of Okeechobee Road and 25th Street, near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. A white cargo van was behind the scooter, traveling east on Okeechobee Road, Maj. Michael Santiago told WPBF's Angela Rozier at a briefing Monday afternoon. The van driver fled the scene and made a U-turn to drive in the wrong direction across the median on Okeechobee Road, but he crashed into the side of a building, the Kings Queens Unisex Salon. The man then ran from the scene. Salon owner Sheila Hampton showed the damage, and is thankful no one was inside at the time. Hampton said she feels for the victim and his family. "His family told me he was just leaving from one of his friend's houses and just going home," she said. A second vehicle, a Toyota pickup truck, was also struck, but no one was injured. Lucie County Sheriff's Office K-9 Unit and Aviation Unit assisted Fort Pierce police and the K-9 Unit in efforts to locate the driver. They are in possession of the van. Police described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark-colored top with light-colored pants or shorts. "So, that in itself proves intent that that person knew exactly what they were doing at the time and was just trying to simply get away," Santiago said. Anyone with information should call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Jupiter Goodwill employee celebrates 19 years on the job during Disability Employment Awareness Month
entry.summary: October marks National Disability Employment Awareness Month, an annual observance recognizing the contributions people with disabilities make to workplaces across the country. The observance dates back to 1945, when it began as a weeklong national recognition of the contributions of people with physical disabilities. WATCH BELOW: Jupiter Goodwill employee celebrates 19 years on the job National Disability Employment Awareness Month highlights value and talent in the workplace In 1988, Congress expanded the commemoration to a month, and it evolved to recognize the importance of increasing employment opportunities for people with disabilities, including those with mental health conditions and other nonobvious disabilities. The U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy, created in 2001, now leads the annual observance. At a Goodwill store in Jupiter, that message can be seen through an employee who has spent nearly two decades putting his own talents to work. WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with Jeffrey McFadden Jr., who has worked at the Jupiter Goodwill for 19 years, but for him, going to work is about much more than earning a paycheck. 'I like to smile at others, uplift people and make other people smile,' McFadden said. Staying with the same employer for nearly two decades is something he and his family take pride in. 'My dad said that is a big achievement, to be in a job for so long, and it's a blessing to be a part of this atmosphere and get to meet really nice people,' McFadden said. He said his path into the workforce included attending Goodwill's transition school, where he received job training. 'I went to the Goodwill transition school where we get job training, and it helped us get jobs,' McFadden said. Abra Joseph, the director of donated goods, said Goodwill's programs are aimed at helping people who face barriers to employment find and maintain jobs. 'Sixty percent of our team members self-identify as having some type of barrier to employment,' Joseph said. entry.title: Florida AG vows public corruption crackdown after Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms conviction - WPBF
entry.summary: Florida AG vows public corruption crackdown after Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms conviction    WPBF
entry.article_text: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is promising a broader crackdown on public corruption following the conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct but acquitted him of bid tampering. The case centered on two vacant, city-owned parcels in Fort Pierce and a nonprofit connected to Mimms’ niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position to benefit the nonprofit and later concealed his involvement. Mimms’ niece served on the nonprofit’s board. The organization received a $500,000 grant from a Catholic charitable organization for a community center that was never built. Uthmeier pointed to the conviction as an example of the state’s efforts to hold public officials accountable. “We want to ensure the public that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take,” Uthmeier said. Uthmeier said the evidence showed that “shenanigans took place” to ensure the nonprofit received the award and that Mimms ultimately covered up his involvement. “He will be punished for abusing his office,” Uthmeier said. Uthmeier said his office’s Public Corruption Unit has more than 25 active investigations or cases underway and described the Mimms case as the first of many public corruption cases the state expects to announce. Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency is making public corruption investigations a priority. “No one is too big, no one is too powerful to be held accountable,” Keefe said. Uthmeier declined to comment on what sentence Mimms should receive. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony punishable by up to five years in prison. Mimms is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. The latest shooting remains under investigation by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office and its Violent Crimes Division, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The number of deadly deputy-involved shootings this year comes as law enforcement agencies continue to face heightened scrutiny over use-of-force incidents and transparency in investigations following fatal encounters. entry.title: Scripps News poll: 43% of voters say they’ve been fooled by AI ads this campaign
entry.summary: Many Americans say theyve been confused or even fooled by political ads using artificial intelligence this campaign season, and want more rules governing how the technology is used, according to a new Scripps News/Talker Research poll. Political Roundtable: AI and political campaign ads More than four-in-ten registered voters say theyve seen something they thought was real in a political ad, only to later find it was AI-generated. Another 30% said they saw something they werent sure was real or AI. Some of the most talked about ads of the campaign have featured AI-generated candidates like Sen. Jon Ossoff in a beauty salon , James Talarico reciting old quotes out of context , and Sherrod Brown overstaying his welcome at a birthday party . More than half of survey respondents (56%) said they have seen Republicans using AI ads, compared with 49% saying they have seen ads for Democrats. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumors And more than three-quarters of voters say there should be rules around how the technology is used in politics. In the absence of federal regulation, states have passed their own laws aimed at curbing the influence of AI or deepfakes in campaign advertising. Some states require disclosures or bar deepfake videos from being published in the weeks leading up to Election Day. But many of the regulations fail to keep up with the evolving use of what can be a cheap and effective new tool. An analysis from the Wesleyan Media Project from early September found AI tools had been used in at least 164 ads, 69% of which did not disclose AI was used. Eighty percent were from Republicans or Republican-leaning groups. Still, a similar amount of voters in both parties say there should be rules around how the technology is used, according to the Scripps News/Talker Research poll, including 77% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans. Concerns about how AI could impact areas outside politics also cut across party lines. Large swaths of the country worry about the impact AI could have on their jobs (61%), government institutions (83%), financial institutions (81%), and their physical safety (57%). Nearly 80% say they see content they believe was generated by AI at least once per day. entry.title: Bear Trap Cognizant Classic ticket prices reduced by more than 50% compared to 2026
entry.summary: Tournament officials announced that admission prices for the Bear Trap at the 2027 Cognizant Classic in the Palm Beaches will be reduced by more than 50% compared to 2026. Right now, fans can secure tickets at $150 for Thursday and Sunday, and $165 for Friday and Saturday. Officials said next year's tournament will also return to a traditional food and beverage model, allowing fans to purchase what they want throughout the venue rather than having it included in the admission price. 'The Bear Trap has always been the social heartbeat of the Cognizant Classic,' said Max Novena, Interim Executive Director of the Cognizant Classic in The Palm Beaches. 'We're bringing back the experience that made it a fan favorite, with more accessible pricing, more room for fans and the electric atmosphere that makes the Bear Trap so special. We want more people to be part of it and these changes are an important step in making that happen.' The offer ends Oct. 29. entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Tuesday. Lenke, 66, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke couldnt accept that the vicitm was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter.

entry.title: Fort Pierce police investigate after body found in Lincoln Park lake - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce police investigate after body found in Lincoln Park lake    WPEC
entry.article_text: A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. An officer was flagged down by a citizen just after 9 a.m. who reported seeing a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said. Officers say they arrived and found a man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him out, but he was pronounced dead. Police identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are working to determine how the man entered the water and what he was doing before his death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified There were no apparent signs of trauma to the man's body, Santiago said, but he noted the body appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the area, speaking with potential witnesses and looking for surveillance footage that could help investigators determine how the man ended up in the lake, per FPPD. Santiago said investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have played a role in where the body was found. It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs were involved. Investigators are waiting for the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death. CBS12 News will provide updates as more information becomes available.

entry.title: Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history
entry.summary: Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies shot and killed a 51-year-old man Tuesday afternoon following a strong-arm robbery report and a pursuit that began in Lake Park, which continued along Interstate 95 and ended in a deadly confrontation near Boynton Beach. On Wednesday, PBSO identified Gregory Dobkins as the man who was fatally shot. Court records show his final encounter with law enforcement was not his first. WATCH BELOW: Man shot by deputies had lengthy criminal history, records show Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history Deputies said Dobkins was a suspect in a strong-arm robbery that happened Monday night when they located him in Lake Park using license plate readers. Deputies and state troopers then pursued him down I-95 before a confrontation in Boynton Beach ended in the shooting. At the scene Tuesday, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw described the moment his deputy fired. 'He was actually in a kneeling position and raised up his hands in the shooting position, and that's when our deputy fired, struck him, and he was neutralized right there,' Bradshaw said. 'During this whole time, he's yelling too at the officers, right? 'You're gonna have to kill me. You're gonna have to kill me, you're gonna have to kill me.'' At the scene, Bradshaw told reporters Dobkins had a lengthy criminal history. 'He's obviously a serious bad guy,' Bradshaw said. WPTV dug through court records across Florida and found a history of theft, assault, drug convictions and other charges that go back decades. Arrest affidavits repeatedly reference a battle with addiction. Most recently in 2025, Dobkins was accused of stealing merchandise from a Walgreens in Sarasota. Deputies wrote that when they confronted Dobkins, he was acting erratically, so they Baker Acted him. Court records show Dobkins pleaded guilty to petit theft and paid a fine. Tuesday's deadly confrontation is still actively under investigation by state and county law enforcement. We're going to keep digging into this to better understand what happened, and will bring details as they are uncovered. entry.title: Motorcyclist killed in Palm Springs crash; drivers urged to avoid the area
entry.summary: A motorcyclist was killed in a crash involving a car Wednesday afternoon in Palm Springs, police said. The Palm Springs Police Department said the crash happened at approximately 2:14 p.m. at the intersection of South Congress Avenue and 2nd Avenue North. entry.title: Martin County moves closer to restoring bus services after sudden shutdown - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County moves closer to restoring bus services after sudden shutdown    WPBF
entry.article_text: Just days after MARTY public bus services abruptly shut down in Martin County, county commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to allow the county administrator to negotiate a new contract with a company that could restore service. The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday’s decision offered a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs last Thursday. “I’m hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work,” Lawrence said. Lawrence was among the drivers impacted when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously operating MARTY, abruptly stopped services last Thursday. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for its decision to discontinue service. During Tuesday’s county commission meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton explained that county officials had spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. “We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us,” Gorton said. According to Gorton, the county evaluated several proposals before identifying MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. One of the county’s priorities during negotiations is bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs following last week’s shutdown. “We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible,” Gorton said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating its previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials say they are hopeful negotiations with MTM Transit can be finalized by the end of this week, potentially allowing buses to begin operating again next week. entry.title: Jury finds Tyreek Hill liable for 2 battery counts, awards $500,000 to the NFL star's estranged wife
entry.summary: A Miami jury on Tuesday found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro ending the high-profile civil trial involving the NFL wide receiver and his estranged wife. Hill, who has played for the NFL's Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025. The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages. The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence. The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and 'treated me like I was, just, a man.' Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called 'false allegations' made by his estranged wife, while saying in one instance he shoved Vaccaro and created a hole in the wall.' Hill, wearing a dark polo shirt on Tuesday, embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself. It wasn't immediately clear what the verdict means for Hill's return to the NFL. He is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated that he could be ready to play by November.

entry.title: Death sentence handed down for 66-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case - WPEC
entry.summary: Death sentence handed down for 66-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case    WPEC
entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

entry.title: $900 a month in fees: West Boca condo owner feels squeeze of rising HOA costs
entry.summary: Stephanie Donner saw my report this week on local leaders discussing HOA fees and assessments in Florida and immediately contacted me. 'It is a problem in the state, to the point where they will put a sign on the highway coming from the north (that says) 'Turnaround,'' she told me outside her West Boca condo on Wednesday. WATCH BELOW: West Boca condo owner says rising HOA fees could force her to move West Boca condo owner says rising HOA fees could force her to move Where she lives, she says her total fees are around $900 a month. 'We're going to have an assessment and, to be honest, a lot of people have already moved,' Donner said. 'This is really tough,' state Sen. Mack Bernard said Tuesday at the HOA Fee forum in West Palm Beach. 'But we dont want another Surfside, but at the same time what we want to do is create new affordable housing.' The discussion comes as Florida communities rank among those with the nation's highest HOA burdens. A Realtor.com analysis previously reported by WPTV found seven of the nation's 10 metro areas with the highest HOA fees relative to estimated mortgage payments were in Florida. Port St. Lucie ranked fifth, while the Sebastian-Vero Beach area ranked ninth. Among the potential solutions raised Tuesday at the forum were additional financial assistance for seniors and more state oversight of HOAs. As for Donner, who is semi-retired, she says that with HOA fees, insurance and overall inflation, she's enduring the situation as long as she has her stay-at-home remote job. 'If I lose that, I have to move,' she said

entry.title: DOJ threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls
entry.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next months midterm elections. A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election. California mails ballots to all registered voters. The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list. If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief, the letter states. RELATED STORY | Records show ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen voters A separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar's office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney's office had investigated during the state's June primary. Unclear how many names DOJ flagged Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan confirmed in a statement that his office received the letter and a thumb drive, along with a hand written note providing a password to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn't yet accessed any files. entry.article_text: Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections.A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election.California mails ballots to all registered voters.The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list.“If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief,” the letter states.RELATED STORY | Records show ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen votersA separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar's office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney's office had investigated during the state's June primary.Unclear how many names DOJ flaggedLos Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan confirmed in a statement that his office received the letter and a thumb drive, along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls.He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn't yet accessed any files. The letter, which Logan made public, does not specify the number of individuals flagged by the federal government.Logan said his office is working with the secretary of state and attorney general's offices to decide how to proceed. Neither of those two offices immediately responded to an emailed request for comment.“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established,” Logan wrote. “And any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”Nationwide search for alleged noncitizen votersThe Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” Weber said in response.That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midtermsAs part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens.The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws.Election official calls 48-hour deadline “unreasonable”Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was “completely unreasonable.”She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter’s registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said.“It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture,” Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn’t have access to the state's detailed voter information.Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has “never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters.”

entry.title: Neighbors ask for solutions on deadly roadway in Port St. Lucie
entry.summary: WPTV is continuing to follow up after the tragic death of a 14-year-old student who was struck by a vehicle on Port St. Lucie Boulevard last Wednesday. Neighbors told WPTV the road can be dangerous during ongoing construction. 'I don't even come down this road no more,' neighbor Selene Gabriele said. I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school. It's very dangerous. A 14-year-old was struck by an SUV on Port St. Lucie Boulevard while walking to school just before sunrise on Oct. 7. He later died from his injuries. Neighbors like Howard Shapiro said the roadway lacks lighting, especially during the early morning and at night. 'I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there, Shapiro said. To protect those kids, pedestrians and drivers, Shapiro said they need lights. 'They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's gonna be helpful. But street lights need to follow, he said. WATCH: WPTV's Tyler Hatfield is listening to neighbors' concerns following the fatal crash Hearing your concerns after fatal crash on Port St Lucie Blvd. The Florida Department of Transportation is in charge of the project along a segment of Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Alcantara Boulevard to Parr Drive. FDOT started construction back in 2025 and, according to its website , crews are widening the road from two to four lanes as well as adding new sidewalks and lights. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said this will make the roadway safer. 'We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway,' Samples said. WPTV asked Samples if city staff can provide any temporary safety measures to address neighbors' concerns. Samples said the work being done is FDOTs responsibility. 'It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it,' Samples said. 'That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can.' WPTV reached out to FDOT to see if there will be any added safety measures in the wake of last week's tragedy. WPTV is still working on getting a response. FDOT said on its website that the SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard Project is expected to be completed in the winter of 2028.

entry.title: Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history
entry.summary: Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies shot and killed a 51-year-old man Tuesday afternoon following a strong-arm robbery report and a pursuit that began in Lake Park, which continued along Interstate 95 and ended in a deadly confrontation near Boynton Beach. On Wednesday, PBSO identified Gregory Dobkins as the man who was fatally shot. Court records show his final encounter with law enforcement was not his first. WATCH BELOW: Man shot by deputies had lengthy criminal history, records show Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history Deputies said Dobkins was a suspect in a strong-arm robbery that happened Monday night when they located him in Lake Park using license plate readers. Deputies and state troopers then pursued him down I-95 before a confrontation in Boynton Beach ended in the shooting. At the scene Tuesday, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw described the moment his deputy fired. 'He was actually in a kneeling position and raised up his hands in the shooting position, and that's when our deputy fired, struck him, and he was neutralized right there,' Bradshaw said. 'During this whole time, he's yelling too at the officers, right? 'You're gonna have to kill me. You're gonna have to kill me, you're gonna have to kill me.'' At the scene, Bradshaw told reporters Dobkins had a lengthy criminal history. 'He's obviously a serious bad guy,' Bradshaw said. WPTV dug through court records across Florida and found a history of theft, assault, drug convictions and other charges that go back decades. Arrest affidavits repeatedly reference a battle with addiction. Most recently in 2025, Dobkins was accused of stealing merchandise from a Walgreens in Sarasota. Deputies wrote that when they confronted Dobkins, he was acting erratically, so they Baker Acted him. Court records show Dobkins pleaded guilty to petit theft and paid a fine. Tuesday's deadly confrontation is still actively under investigation by state and county law enforcement. We're going to keep digging into this to better understand what happened, and will bring details as they are uncovered. entry.title: Former Melbourne police officer sentenced to death for killing Fort Pierce motorcycle mechanic
entry.summary: A former Melbourne police officer and Treasure Coast first responder has been sentenced to death. Otto Lenke was found guilty in May of shooting and killing Richard Benson inside the victim's bike shop, Fast Frank's , back in February 2021. WATCH BELOW: Former police officer sentenced to death for killing mechanic Former police officer sentenced to death for killing mechanic The crime happened just down the street from Fort Pierce Police Department headquarters. Prosecutors showed the jury surveillance video of the crime during the trial back in May. Lenke not only shot Benson, but spread denatured alcohol over his body and set him on fire while he was still alive. As to a motive, prosecutors noted Benson was dating a woman that Lenke had once been romantically involved with. Assistant State Attorney Brandon White told WPTV that justice was served and he's pleased that this part of the legal process is done.

entry.title: Suspected fentanyl trafficker arrested after 115 mph chase on I-95 in St. Lucie County - WPBF
entry.summary: Suspected fentanyl trafficker arrested after 115 mph chase on I-95 in St. Lucie County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A suspected fentanyl trafficker is behind bars after investigators say he sold drugs to a person who later died of an overdose, then led law enforcement on a high-speed chase that reached 115 mph and ended in Martin County. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro identified the suspect as 43-year-old James Arthur Green, who he said is a 10-time convicted felon. According to the sheriff, the investigation began after a fatal fentanyl overdose on Oct. Detectives used the victim’s phone to contact Green, who allegedly returned to the victim’s home Tuesday to deliver more fentanyl. Investigators say Green even sent a picture to the victim’s phone showing where he had left the drugs, unaware that he had been communicating with law enforcement the entire time. "Obviously, he didn’t know that this person had passed away. We were communicating with them," Del Toro said. Later that day, investigators say Green attempted to sell more fentanyl during an undercover operation. When detectives moved in to arrest him, Green fled, striking an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office cruiser before leading law enforcement on a pursuit down Interstate 95. Authorities say the chase reached speeds of 115 mph and continued into Martin County. The pursuit eventually ended near Kanner Highway after Florida Highway Patrol troopers deployed stop sticks and performed a PIT maneuver to stop Green’s vehicle. Del Toro emphasized the dangers of fentanyl and the importance of removing suspected traffickers from the community. This is killing our citizens and our community and preying upon people that have substance abuse problems," Del Toro said. "So I’m very, very happy this person’s off the streets right now." Green now faces multiple drug-related charges, along with additional charges connected to the pursuit. He is being held on a $440,000 bond. entry.title: Suspected fentanyl supplier linked to overdose death arrested after chase on I-95
entry.summary: A suspected drug trafficker linked to a deadly fentanyl overdose investigation is behind bars after investigators say he fled from detectives, hit a law enforcement vehicle and led authorities on a high-speed chase on I-95 in St. Lucie and Martin counties. Investigators said the arrest of James Arthur Green, 43, came after a weeks-long narcotics investigation that also uncovered a suspected connection to a fatal fentanyl overdose. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, detectives with the Special Investigations Division conducted multiple undercover purchases of drugs, gathering evidence during those operations that identified Green as the suspected supplier of fentanyl to a person who later died from an overdose. On Oct. 13, detectives used the deceased victim's cellphone during another controlled narcotics operation and placed an order for fentanyl. Investigators said Green returned to the victim's residence, delivered about two grams of fentanyl and sent a photograph showing where he left the drugs. Later that day, detectives conducted a separate undercover operation in which Green allegedly participated in a transaction involving about two ounces of fentanyl and one pound of methamphetamine. When detectives attempted to arrest him, Green fled, allegedly hitting a sheriff's office vehicle and fleeing onto southbound I-95. Authorities said the pursuit reached speeds of approximately 115 mph. During the chase, detectives reported seeing Green throw suspected narcotics and a cellphone out of his vehicle. The Florida Highway Patrol and Martin County Sheriff's Office joined the pursuit as it entered Martin County. Troopers deployed stop sticks before performing a PIT maneuver near Kanner Highway, bringing the chase to an end. Investigators recovered the one pound of methamphetamine and two ounces of fentanyl associated with the controlled purchase, along with an additional 22 grams of methamphetamine, two grams of crack cocaine and one gram of fentanyl. entry.title: 'FIRST OF MANY': Attorney General discusses Nick Mimms conviction, warns of more corruption cases
entry.summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier highlighted the recent conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms at a press conference Wednesday, calling it the first major outcome from the state's newly created public corruption unit and warning that more investigations are underway across Florida. Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier said public officials who abuse their positions for personal gain will face increased scrutiny from his office and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE). 'Public officials are held to an even higher standard,' Uthmeier said. 'If you work in a city hall, serve on a commission, if you hold public office or work for a state agency, you have a duty to serve the public and not use your job to enrich yourself.' Last week, a St. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, but acquitted him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024, Mimms used his position to benefit a nonprofit organization on whose board his niece served by helping secure the land deal and later concealing his involvement. During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Mimms failed to disclose his familial relationship and took steps to influence and cover up the transaction. Uthmeier said the case represented the type of conduct the state's public corruption unit was created to investigate. 'The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up,' Uthmeier said. According to Uthmeier, the nonprofit later received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from a Catholic charitable organization for planned development on the property, though he said the infrastructure project never materialized. 'We'll keep digging,' Uthmeier said. 'I think more facts will come to light as to where that money was going.' Uthmeier said since the public corruption unit was launched, investigators have opened more than 25 active public corruption investigations or cases statewide. 'This is the first big announcement,' he said. 'You'll see many to come in the weeks ahead as we wrap up our evidence and begin to press charges against people that have abused their office, that have abused the public trust.' During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Mimms failed to disclose his familial relationship and took steps to influence and cover up the transaction.Uthmeier said the case represented the type of conduct the state's public corruption unit was created to investigate."The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up," Uthmeier said.According to Uthmeier, the nonprofit later received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from a Catholic charitable organization for planned development on the property, though he said the infrastructure project never materialized."We'll keep digging," Uthmeier said. "I think more facts will come to light as to where that money was going."Uthmeier said since the public corruption unit was launched, investigators have opened more than 25 active public corruption investigations or cases statewide."This is the first big announcement," he said. "You'll see many to come in the weeks ahead as we wrap up our evidence and begin to press charges against people that have abused their office, that have abused the public trust."FDLE Larry Keefe said the agency is making public corruption investigations a top priority."When the people of Florida lose their sense of trust in their institutions, it's death by a thousand cuts," Keefe said. Sentencing for Mimms is expected at a later date."This will be the first of many, sadly," Uthmeier said. "I hope we don't have to do too many, but we'll do as many as necessary to ensure the public knows that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers, and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take."

entry.title: Road, flight restrictions set to take effect near Mar-a-Lago this weekend
entry.summary: A major stretch of South Ocean Boulevard in Palm Beach is scheduled to close Friday morning until further notice, prompting traffic changes for residents and commuters in the area. entry.summary: A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership, the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters. More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol. When investigative reporter Kate Hussey asked whether he believed that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes."I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. One showed firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees.Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation.The three have maintained the activity was consensual and "all in good fun.""It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson previously told WPTV."We're all still friends," Boudrias said.Their terminations sparked pushback from firefighters and members of the community, which eventually led to the union's no-confidence vote."The amount that voted no confidence really sends a message that we have, in their opinion, a lack of confidence in their leadership," union representative Ryan Sapp said.Sapp is representing the three firefighters in their fight for reinstatement. entry.title: Santaluces star Jayvon Dawson transforms from QB to elite edge rusher on his way to the University of Miami
entry.summary: In life, they say it's not how you start; it's how you finish, and for Jayvon Dawson, his football start is one of a kind. 'Back in Little League, I first played as a quarterback trying to dab on everybody,' said Dawson. WATCH BELOW: Jayvon Dawson went from QB to elite edge rusher at Santaluces, earning offer from Miami From QB to the U: Jayvon Dawson's path to Miami Dawson was a solid quarterback, but it wasnt until he got to high school at Santaluces that he was humbled. 'My coaches were saying, 'You're not going D1 playing quarterback,'' said Dawson. Dawson is 6-foot-4 and more than 200 pounds, so coaches got creative in his first three years on where they'd pay him. 'He played receiver before we were able to get him on the defensive side of the ball,' head coach Samuel Putmon said. That defensive side of the ball is where he shined. His junior year, he was a man amongst boys and had nearly every school you could think of calling. 'Miami, (the University of North Carolina), Georgia and many others,' said Dawson. Dawson was a game-wrecker the last two seasons, getting to the quarterback at ease and stopping almost every run game the Chiefs faced. He was so good the University of Miami pulled out the big dogs during his recruitment. '(Defensive coordinator Corey) Hetherman and (defensive line coach) Jason Taylor,' said Dawson. Dawson wasn't born when Taylor was dominating the NFL for the Miami Dolphins, so he didnt even know who was recruiting him until days later. 'I was looking up d-ends trying to work some moves on my game and get better at my game, and then he popped up playing for the Dolphins. That's how I started to know him,' said Dawson. Star-struck by his lead recruiter and the Hurricanes' facilities, Dawson made his coach a promise. 'I already told my coach if Miami offers me, I'm fully committed,' Dawson said. During a visit to Coral Gables, Miami did just that and offered the three-star edge rusher. Dawson committed to the school on the spot. 'I kept God first, always kept him first, I just kept going and being consistent and disciplined, said Dawson. That positive mindset has him ready to become an early enrollee at The U this December, and before he steps on the campus, his head coach has glowing reviews for the Us coaches and fans. 'He's a great kid, a humble kid, a hard worker who does what's asked of him. It's easy to coach kids like that,' Putmon said.

entry.title: 'We don't need to lose another child': Port St. Lucie residents push for safer walking routes - WPBF
entry.summary: 'We don't need to lose another child': Port St. Lucie residents push for safer walking routes    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie continues building sidewalks across the city, residents advocating for safer school bus stops and routes say more immediate measures are needed to protect children walking along busy roads. Lucie resident and grandmother, has been pushing city officials for safer bus stops, pedestrian stop signs and painted walkways, saying children should not have to risk their lives getting to and from school. Green said her concerns grew after watching her granddaughter and other children navigate traffic near their neighborhood off Southwest Paar Drive, where a sidewalk only exists on one side of the street. Green said once the bus drops the children off, the bus driver helps them cross the street to where the sidewalk is. However, the children who live on the opposite side of the street then have to cross back over without help. "Once the bus stopped and the kids were walking, cars were flying by. Literally, if you crossed your foot across that line, a child would have been run over or an adult. So that started my campaign to email our city officials, transportation officials, and we did get an opportunity to speak," she said. Green said she has continued communicating with city officials and transportation officials about potential safety improvements. She is calling for more sidewalks, pedestrian stop signs and marked walkways. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "Kids should be able to just walk along the street and make it home safely, walk to school safely," Green said. She mentioned the recent tragic incident in which a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school in Port St. "My heart goes out to the family. I, too, have lost a child before, so I understand that grief. When I met with city officials right there at the corner, I literally said, 'We don't need to lose another child,'" she told WPBF. Sidewalk projects underway across the city The city says sidewalks are currently being installed through its Capital Improvement Projects and Sidewalk Master Plan. Active projects include Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Alcantarra to Paar, Floresta Drive from Crosstown Parkway to Prima Vista, Kestor Drive, Volucia Drive and Lakehurst Drive. Recently completed projects include sidewalks on Abingdon Avenue, Import Drive, Brescia Street and Grand Drive, as well as Berkshire Boulevard Phase 1 and a Veterans Memorial Parkway connection to the Publix plaza and post office. Upcoming projects include California Boulevard from Crosstown Parkway to Prima Vista and the Peacock Trail at O.L. Park, from Dreyfuss Boulevard to Open View Drive. City officials say the public works department continues to evaluate existing priorities and identify additional locations for future improvements. An updated plan, including proposed future sidewalk locations, is expected to be presented to the City Council for approval in 2027. What about safety before sidewalks are built? The city says it has met with the St. Lucie County School Board as part of the master plan review to discuss school bus stops. City officials say the school board determines bus stop locations, which can change annually based on transportation needs and where children live. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The city also says crosswalks are evaluated as part of new projects. Under federal accessibility requirements, crosswalks must connect to compliant sidewalks and curb ramps at both ends, meaning they cannot be installed independently where accessible pedestrian infrastructure is absent. A push for more neighborhood input According to the city, the previous sidewalk master plan prioritized major roadways, particularly within 2 miles of schools, with the goal of connecting existing sidewalks rather than building isolated sections. The updated plan is expected to expand those connections into more neighborhoods, while continuing to prioritize heavily traveled areas and routes connecting schools, parks and recreational destinations. A call for action For Green, the issue goes beyond her own family. She said every resident has a connection to a child who could face similar dangers. She started a petition asking the city to implement several safety measures to protect children, including: Immediate transverse pedestrian crosswalks Immediate in-street pedestrian crossing signs Speed bumps to permanently slow down reckless drivers "Collectively, together, we’re stronger," Green said. The petition can be found here.

entry.title: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case - WPEC
entry.summary: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case    WPEC
entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

entry.title: Celebrities tee off for a cause at Par for the Culture golf tournament in Greenacres, Florida
entry.summary: GREENACRES, Fla. Golf, celebrities, and community impact will come together on Monday, October 19th as Par for the Culture celebrity golf tournament takes over Palm Beach National Golf Country Club, raising awareness and support for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County. The event, organized by Darren Wingate, will bring together professional athletes, celebrities, influencers, and community leaders for a day of golf with a purpose. Proceeds from the tournament will benefit The Lord's Place, a Palm Beach County nonprofit organization that provides housing assistance, supportive services and programs designed to help individuals and families experiencing homelessness rebuild their lives. For Wingate, the mission goes beyond the golf course. The tournament is designed to use the influence of sports and entertainment to bring attention to affordable housing, homelessness and the importance of community involvement. The event also aims to introduce new audiences to golf while creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to connect through a shared cause. The Lord's Place works to address homelessness through services that include street outreach, housing support, employment training and programs that help people achieve greater independence. Organizers hope the tournament will encourage athletes and community leaders to use their platforms to support housing initiatives, not just in Palm Beach County, but in communities across the country. entry.title: 'We need help': Martin County transit cuts put strain on United Way's Ride United program
entry.summary: The United Way of Martin County is calling on the community for support as transit services for residents face mounting challenges. The organization says the MARTY bus shutdown last week was just the tip of the iceberg. The United Way has been seeing an increased need for transit services following state budget cuts earlier this year. WATCH BELOW: United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requests United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requests Henry Hayden relies on community transit services to get to and from work. As an adult on the autism spectrum, he and his mom, Leigh Hayden, say his job gives him purpose. 'It feels like I'm independent. I can do stuff on my own,' Henry Hayden said. 'I like working because I like to talk to people. I like to get some knowledge.' 'The gifts that come with having Henry employed they're so huge,' Leigh Hayden said. In August, state budget cuts reduced funding for Community Coach, a program that helps disabled people like Henry get around. The cuts meant any disabled riders under age 70 had to find a new means of transportation. 'I said I don't know what to do,' Henry Hayden said. 'It was like having the bottom drop out. This is our lifeline, and until you know that, you really don't understand how important something like transportation is,' Leigh Hayden said. Carol Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of the United Way of Martin County, says many turned to the organization's 'Ride United' program following the Community Coach cuts. It is the same program that Martin County residents are now using amid the MARTY Bus shutdown. 'When that closed, everything fell on the United Way. It's just really put a strain on us financially,' Houwaart-Diez said. Last year alone, 'Ride United' provided over 7,600 trips. In the last three and a half months, the organization says it has already completed over 2,800 trips. 'We need help, we need people to really start looking at how we can get that funding restored because we shouldn't be the only solution,' Houwaart-Diez said. Without services like 'Ride United,' people like Henry Hayden would lose their independence. 'I'm eternally grateful,' Henry Hayden said. 'Transportation is the piece of the puzzle that hooks to self-esteem to groceries to purpose to his character,' Leigh Hayden said. The United Way is calling on the community for help to support the increased need for community transit services. This story was reported on-air by a journalist

As an adult on the autism spectrum, he and his mom, Leigh Hayden, say his job gives him purpose."It feels like I'm independent. I can do stuff on my own," Henry Hayden said. "I like working because I like to talk to people. I like to get some knowledge.""The gifts that come with having Henry employed — they're so huge," Leigh Hayden said.In August, state budget cuts reduced funding for Community Coach, a program that helps disabled people like Henry get around. The cuts meant any disabled riders under age 70 had to find a new means of transportation."I said I don't know what to do," Henry Hayden said."It was like having the bottom drop out. This is our lifeline, and until you know that, you really don't understand how important something like transportation is," Leigh Hayden said.Carol Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of the United Way of Martin County, says many turned to the organization's "Ride United" program following the Community Coach cuts. It is the same program that Martin County residents are now using amid the MARTY Bus shutdown."When that closed, everything fell on the United Way. It's just really put a strain on us financially," Houwaart-Diez said.Last year alone, "Ride United" provided over 7,600 trips. In the last three and a half months, the organization says it has already completed over 2,800 trips."We need help, we need people to really start looking at how we can get that funding restored because we shouldn't be the only solution," Houwaart-Diez said.Without services like "Ride United," people like Henry Hayden would lose their independence."I'm eternally grateful," Henry Hayden said."Transportation is the piece of the puzzle that hooks to self-esteem to groceries to purpose to his character," Leigh Hayden said.The United Way is calling on the community for help to support the increased need for community transit services.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Palm Springs Police Department said the crash happened at approximately 2:14 p.m. at the intersection of South Congress Avenue and 2nd Avenue North. Police have not released the identity of the person who died or provided details about what led to the collision. entry.title: West Palm Beach residents push back on high-rise development along Flagler Drive
entry.summary: More than 100 people gathered Wednesday evening to weigh in on development rules covering 12 acres along South Flagler Drive, where residents say high-rise construction is increasing traffic and encroaching on historic neighborhoods. The city of West Palm Beach held the public workshop at St. Catherine Greek Orthodox Church to collect feedback on zoning regulations within the South Flagler Overlay District. WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache attended the workshop and spoke with residents about their concerns. City staff focused the discussion on parking, building density and height. Residents, however, used the meeting to voice broader concerns about what they described as excessive development along the waterfront. The traffic has increased exponentially, one attendee said. West Palm Beach residents push back on Flagler waterfront development Residents question neighborhood impact West Palm Beach has undergone a major transformation, with new construction reshaping its downtown and waterfront. Several residents said they do not oppose development but want city leaders to consider its cumulative effects on traffic, infrastructure and surrounding neighborhoods. Im not against developing and making better and bringing value to our neighborhood, but can we take into consideration the overall impact? one resident asked. WPTV identified at least six new or planned developments along Flagler Drive. Longtime residents said the projects are changing the character of the waterfront and could place increasingly tall buildings next to historic homes. If we want high-rises, they have a place, downtown or near downtown, resident Amy Triggs said. Its not appropriate to build a high-rise near a 1920s neighborhood. Resident Jeff Eagle said he opposes a building approaching 200 feet in height near a historic neighborhood. I dont want a 190-some-odd-foot-tall building in a historic neighborhood, Eagle said. City reviewing waterfront zoning In July, the West Palm Beach City Commission paused waterfront redevelopment approvals for six months while the city reviews its zoning regulations. City officials said property owners have development rights, but the review is intended to keep residents informed and give the community an opportunity to comment before projects move forward. The city is expected to review feedback collected through its community survey on Nov. 4. The majority of the people all want the same thing, Eagle said. entry.title: Florida ordered license plate readers off state roads. Why does Palm Beach County still have them?
entry.summary: The Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office says it has received an exemption allowing the agency to continue using license plate reader cameras on state roads, despite a statewide push to remove the technology from those roads. PBSO has used the technology for years, including in searches for criminal suspects and endangered people.
