entry.article_text: A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office.The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Man found dead after St. Lucie County barricade situationDeputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said.Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home.According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside.During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot.Knowing a woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said.Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community.Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie residents weigh in on proposed Prima Vista Boulevard safety changes - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie residents weigh in on proposed Prima Vista Boulevard safety changes    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie community members had a chance to learn more about and comment on proposed safety changes to Prima Vista Boulevard during a county information session at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center Thursday. The proposal focuses on the stretch between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. It would replace the center turn lane with a raised median and add landscaping designed to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down. A majority of the community members spoke out against the plan, saying they don't believe the changes would improve safety. County officials say the changes are intended to improve safety, reduce crashes, and help slow traffic along the corridor. "We understand it's not popular. That's why we have these," said St. Lucie County engineer Dan Zrallack. "We're taking away the ease of access for people who live along this corridor. There's a lot of driveways. There's a lot of residences that have historically been able to turn directly into their driveway. It's no longer safe to do that. We have to control the traffic so that we have less accidents." County staff estimate the project could cost about $6.1 million dollars, but don't know where that money would come from yet. See also: Jupiter woman sues DoorDash, alleges delivery driver sexually assaulted her County leaders said feedback from the meeting will help shape the project. The proposal is in the early stages. Lucie County still needs to design the roadway, and identify funding sources before any work can move forward. Residents who couldn’t attend the workshop can review plans and submit comments to Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

entry.title: Local court leaders urge residents to respond to jury summonses as turnout drops
entry.summary: Court officials in Floridas 19th Judicial Circuit are warning people who ignore jury duty summonses that they could face fines and other legal consequences. The circuit serves Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie, and Okeechobee counties. Officials say low response rates are making it harder to select juries and can delay court proceedings. At a recent WPTV Lets Hear It meetup in Okeechobee , Jerald D. Bryant, clerk of circuit court and comptroller, spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the problem. WATCH: Treasure Coast courts crack down on jury duty no-shows We just ask one thing, and we don't ask you to do it often, but people just ignore them, Bryant said. The numbers illustrate the concern. In April 2026, 300 people were summoned for jury duty, but only 60 reported. That means just one in five people showed up. Bryant said a jury summons is a court order and ignoring it can have legal consequences. It is contempt of court because a jury summons is a court order to appear, Bryant said. Why jury duty participation matters Court officials say low turnout can make it difficult to assemble a jury, potentially delaying trials and affecting defendants waiting for their cases to be heard, as well as victims and their families. Chief Judge Charles A. Schwab told WPTV that higher response rates could also help the court use its resources more efficiently. If we knew that that return rate was going to be 75% to 85%, that money could be diverted to things that we use in the community would rather be spending those on, Schwab said. What happens if you ignore a jury summons? Court leaders say they plan to enforce the consequences for people who fail to appear for jury duty. People who ignore their summonses could receive an order requiring them to explain their absence to a judge. They could face a $100 fine and still be required to serve on a jury. Failing to appear for that court hearing could lead to a bench warrant and potential arrest. Diamond Litty, public defender for the 19th judicial circuit, encouraged anyone with questions or a legitimate issue preventing them from attending to contact the court. I encourage everyone to do the right thing, to not ignore it. If you have an issue, make a phone call. There's a number on the summons, Litty said. 'Please do the right thing.' Chief Judge Schwab said the court intends to enforce the consequences moving forward. Failure to show up there is a consequence, and the courts are going to be enforcing those consequence

entry.summary: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest    WPEC
entry.article_text: 27-year-old man is accused of exposing himself in multiple incidents involving women walking alone on the Seaway Bridge in Fort Pierce, and police say two victims identified him as the suspect. Kyle Kennedy was arrested Friday after an investigation by the Fort Pierce Police Department into multiple reports of indecent exposure on the bridge. Investigators reviewed previous reports and spotted patterns linking the incidents, then interviewed victims and conducted photo lineups, police said. See also: Florida divers remove record 36,187 invasive lionfish in statewide challenge Two victims positively identified Kennedy during the lineups, leading to his arrest, according to police. "It's just crazy to know that there's something like that going on," Leidi Cruz of Fort Pierce. "I've never had any experience like that. We walk here regularly and we've never had any issues." Kennedy faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation. Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or has information about the incidents to call the FPPD at 772-467-6800 . Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

entry.title: Man who claimed woman was possessed by the devil sentenced for Vero Beach hotel attack - cw34.com
entry.summary: Man who claimed woman was possessed by the devil sentenced for Vero Beach hotel attack    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman in a hotel room and throwing water on her after she tried to leave has been sentenced to nine months in jail. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office say they were called to Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach on December 23, 2025, after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. See also: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, who was visibly wet and shaken. Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She also told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him. Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. Investigators also spoke with a witness who said she heard a woman yelling, Stop, Rape, Help Me, before seeing the man appear to drag the woman back into the room. Lagola was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery and was held in St. Lucie County Jail until his sentencing and was given 297 days time served.

entry.title: Blue Repose launches Juno Beach pilot program to help public safety professionals recover
entry.summary: Blue Repose Foundation is launching a pilot program designed to help law enforcement officers and other public safety professionals recover from occupational stress through weekly float sessions, peer support and coping techniques. The startup nonprofit introduced the program at Float8 in Delray Beach, where Blue Repose Founder and President Bridget Coghlan discussed the pressures public safety professionals can encounter and the stigma that may prevent some from seeking support. With our field, of course, we're exposed to traumas, long shift hours, and things of that nature, Coghlan said. We don't like to say mental health, so we just want to take care of the person and give them resources to do so within their professional life and their personal life at home. Five participants will enter a monthlong pilot Coghlan said the pilot will include five participants during its initial monthlong run at Transitions Wellness and Performance Center in Juno Beach. They'll get a float session, one per week, followed by peer support and other coping decompression techniques to follow and hopefully it'll help them out, Coghlan said. The program is part of Blue Repose Foundations developing mission to provide private, nonclinical restorative opportunities to law enforcement officers, corrections professionals and others working in public safety. Blue Repose says the foundation is being established in Martin County, with an initial focus on serving the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Blue Repose seeks community support Kristen Neves, the foundations director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot. We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going, Neves said. We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported. Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website. How the Float8 Delray cabins work Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods. Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation. Kristen Neves, the foundation’s director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot.“We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going,” Neves said. “We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported.”Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website.Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods.Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation.“By reducing the effects of gravity and external stimulation on the body, it helps induce a meditative state, downregulate your nervous system, and help you recover from those stressful situations that our law enforcement officers face so often,” Beck said.Blue Repose describes the float experience as one component of a broader program that will include peer support and additional coping and decompression techniques.Public safety professionals can encounter trauma, long shifts, and sustained stress while serving their communities. Blue Repose’s pilot reflects an effort to give participants structured time to decompress while connecting them with support beyond the float cabin.The initial program will allow Blue Repose to begin evaluating its approach with a small group of participants as the nonprofit works to secure community funding.The foundation’s broader goal is to help professionals take care of themselves in both their working and personal lives while making recovery a more accepted part of public service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award. WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-old The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention. "It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl." That little girl was 3-year-old Luna. Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her. "I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said. Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. "You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool." A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue. "Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital. Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help. "It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said. Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters. This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue. Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award in recognition of her actions. "Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition. According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award. For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up. "What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said. Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby." For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude. "I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said. For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life. entry.title: Florida's Turnpike South blocked in St. Lucie County after truck fire, separate crash
entry.summary: Traffic remains slow on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County after a truck fire and a separate crash near the same location Tuesday morning. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area prompted another full closure. As of 11:30 a.m., one southbound lane has reopened, though motorists should continue to expect significant delays near mile marker 161. It's unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WPTV has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated as more information becomes available.

entry.title: What's next for Boca Raton? Mayor outlines plan after city manager's resignation
entry.summary: The City of Boca Raton is preparing for a leadership transition after City Manager Mark Sohaney announced he is stepping down after roughly 13 months in the position. City officials say an interim city manager could be selected by mid-November ahead of his expected departure. Sohaney is leaving to join the University of Maryland Global Campus as senior vice president for global military operations, according to Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson. The move returns Sohaney to a field closely tied to his background as a retired U.S. Navy captain. The resignation comes as Boca Raton continues work on several major initiatives, including plans for a proposed new police headquarters and other long-term projects expected to shape the city's future. Mayor says city remains on stable footing Mayor Andy Thomson acknowledged it is difficult to see Sohaney leave but said he understands the opportunity. 'For him to have the opportunity to go back and work in a capacity supporting military families and supporting our military makes perfect sense,' Thomson said. Despite the leadership change, Thomson said residents should remain confident in the city's direction. 'Leadership continues to be very strong and the city's in very good hands,' he said. According to Thomson, city staff and elected leaders are prepared to continue advancing major projects while seeking public input and voter approval where required. Leadership changes draw attention Sohaney's departure follows a period of significant turnover within city leadership. In March, WPTV reported on a major shakeup that included the departures of Boca Raton's police chief and two deputy city managers. The latest announcement has prompted some residents to question the city's leadership stability and what comes next for one of Palm Beach County's largest municipalities. When asked how residents can be assured the next city manager will remain in the role long term, Thomson pointed to Boca Raton's history of retaining top leaders for decades. entry.title: Florida secures arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown
entry.summary: Florida has secured an arrest warrant charging former Cuban leader Ral Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with the 1996 shootdown of two unarmed Brothers to the Rescue planes that killed four men, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday. The state case comes months after federal prosecutors indicted Castro and others over the same attack, raising questions about what the new Florida prosecution could mean alongside the existing federal case. WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman spoke with a former state attorney about the practical impact of the state charges and with a Cuban American woman whose family had a close connection to Brothers to the Rescue. 'It was not an accident what happened. It was murder,' Uthmeier said Monday. 'The evidence makes abundantly clear that there was a conspiracy.' The Florida Attorney General's Office said its Office of Statewide Prosecution and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement secured the warrant. The state charges Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. entry.article_text: Florida has secured an arrest warrant charging former Cuban leader Raúl Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with the 1996 shootdown of two unarmed Brothers to the Rescue planes that killed four men, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday.The state case comes months after federal prosecutors indicted Castro and others over the same attack, raising questions about what the new Florida prosecution could mean alongside the existing federal case.WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman spoke with a former state attorney about the practical impact of the state charges and with a Cuban American woman whose family had a close connection to Brothers to the Rescue."It was not an accident what happened. It was murder," Uthmeier said Monday. "The evidence makes abundantly clear that there was a conspiracy."The Florida Attorney General's Office said its Office of Statewide Prosecution and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement secured the warrant. The state charges Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.The allegations date back to Feb. 24, 1996, when a Cuban military aircraft shot down two unarmed civilian planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue over international waters.The four men killed were Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr.Brothers to the Rescue was a Miami-based Cuban exile organization whose missions included searching for Cuban migrants at sea."Raúl Castro called for the planes to be shot down," Uthmeier said. "He called for murder."According to the state attorney general's office, Castro is accused of participating in a conspiracy involving Cuban spies operating in South Florida who supplied intelligence to Havana.The arrest warrant affidavit alleges the goal was to kill people aboard the Brothers to the Rescue aircraft "using information provided by spies operating in Miami-Dade and Monroe counties."Florida's case does not stand alone.Federal prosecutors announced an indictment against Castro in May stemming from the same 1996 shootdown. The state prosecution is proceeding alongside that federal case.Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told WPTV that federal authorities would ordinarily take the lead on a case such as this."The federal government usually takes the lead on matters like this," Aronberg said.Aronberg questioned how much practical effect a state prosecution would have if Castro were ultimately brought to the United States."If he is brought to the United States to face justice at all, it'll be by the United States to face federal charges in a federal court and then get federal prison time," Aronberg said.Uthmeier, however, argued Monday that the state warrant has consequences. He said it could affect Castro's ability to travel internationally if he enters a country willing and legally able to assist with an arrest or extradition. Such an outcome would depend on the country's laws, applicable extradition arrangements and federal cooperation.The state announcement also brought questions about its timing.Monday marked the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade County, where Uthmeier is seeking election as attorney general.Aronberg told WPTV he believes politics played a role."I think the timing so close to the election is not a coincidence," Aronberg said. "This is a splash that the attorney general wanted to make, and perhaps it's justified under state law. But the timing does indicate that politics came into play here."Uthmeier's opponent also criticized the timing in a statement to WPTV."If we can arrest the murderous Raúl Castro from Tallahassee, I will be the first to do it as Attorney General," the statement said in part.The opponent argued that Uthmeier "somehow chose the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade to make this announcement" and called it "a smokescreen to distract from Hope Florida and Alligator Alcatraz."Beyond the legal and political questions, the case remains deeply personal for members of South Florida's Cuban American community.Hoffman spoke with Mirta Luaces, who said she fled Cuba 65 years ago in search of freedom."I came here in search of freedom, the freedom that I have lost in Cuba," Luaces said.Her son, she said, was a pilot with Brothers to the Rescue and could have been flying with the organization the day of the shootdown."The reason why he wasn't flying that day is because he had moved to Daytona, and he wasn't coming every week," Luaces said. "But otherwise, he could have been one of the victims."Luaces told WPTV she welcomed the new charges and hopes Cuba's political system will someday change."I hope that one day the political system in Cuba will change," Luaces said. "We will have free elections, and democracy will take place in Havana, in Cuba again."Thirty years after the shootdown, Florida's prosecution adds a state case to an already active federal effort to hold Castro accountable. Whether Castro will ever appear in a U.S. courtroom remains an open practical question, but the new warrant adds another legal avenue tied to a case that has remained significant to South Florida's Cuban exile community for decades.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool
entry.summary: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award. WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-old Woman Honored After Using CPR to Save 3-Year-Old Girl | WPTV The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention. 'It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses,' Isler said. 'And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl.' That little girl was 3-year-old Luna. 'I jumped in and grabbed her' Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her. 'I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue,' Isler said. Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. 'You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby,' Isler said. 'I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool.' A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue. 'Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded,' Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital. 'It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time,' Hernandez said. Police said officers noticed signs of impairment, including slurred speech, lethargy and difficulty maintaining balance. Her breath test result was 0.130, according to the department. James Kirby, 81, was arrested Friday after police received a report of a potentially impaired driver leaving a restaurant. Officers stopped his pickup truck on SW Becker Road after seeing it change lanes without signaling and brake suddenly at a green light, police said. Officers reported that Kirby had slurred speech, watery eyes and difficulty maintaining balance. His breath test result was 0.123, according to police. Tamra Goodman, 57, was arrested Sunday after officers responded to a single-vehicle crash on SE Port St. Lucie Boulevard, west of U.S. Police said her Mustang had struck a curb and was damaged and inoperable. Goodman told officers she had left a restaurant and had three vodka and club soda drinks, police said. Her breath test result was 0.227. entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: The man convicted of killing an Indian River County deputy nearly 40 years ago is scheduled to be executed Tuesday. William Reaves, 77, is set to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke . Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant Sept. According to court records, Cpl. Richard Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. During the encounter, a gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives in Albany, Reaves admitted to the shooting. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he said, according to a transcript filed by the state. When a detective asked why he would not give up the gun, Reaves said he was a convicted felon and feared prison. I know if I got caught with that gun, and the man take me down there, I’m gonna get a mandatory three years already for the gun, he said. Reaves also told detectives, I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked. Prosecutors have long argued the shooting was premeditated. Court records show the deputy was running away when he was shot, and the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. See also: Florida secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 shootdown Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week, and a request for the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case is still pending. His attorneys and supporters, including a group of military veterans, have asked DeSantis to spare his life, pointing to his service in Vietnam. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented Reaves in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

entry.summary: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida's eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation's aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida's eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation's aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful.The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida's method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution.Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. Supreme Court.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: A pumpkin wonderland in the Florida sunshine: Inside the fall fun at Bedner's Farm
entry.summary: Just outside Boynton Beach, Bedner's Farm offers a little bit of country, a whole lot of fall fun and a reminder that autumn magic doesn't require chilly weather. Fall fun in the Florida sunshine: Inside Bedner's Farm near Boynton Beach At the family-owned South Florida staple tucked away in west Boynton Beach, even the goats get in on the hospitality. According to Judi Brooker, who has been sharing the farm's charm with visitors for more than a decade, they're a crowd favorite. 'They're so soft, and everybody loves the goats,' Brooker said. I mentioned that the little kids probably love them. 'And by little kids, everybody under the age of 100,' Brooker joked. Bedner's is one of South Florida's last family-owned markets, with a farming legacy that stretches back generations. 'A lot of people don't realize there is life in west Boynton off 441,' Brooker said. 'I know I live here!' More than 50 years ago, Arthur and Henrietta Bedner brought their Pennsylvania farming roots to South Florida, trading harsh winters for a warmer climate and new opportunities. 'They came from farming families in Pennsylvania, but they'd had enough of the winter,' Brooker said. The family began farming in the area in the mid-20th century before purchasing the property that would become home to the farm visitors know today. Their mission remains simple: grow fresh, flavorful produce that's affordable, too. And there's plenty growing here. The farm grows about 60 crops, including tomatoes, corn, strawberries, broccoli, kale, lettuce, cauliflower, peppers and zucchini. The farm also grows sunflowers, adding a splash of color to the agricultural landscape. October is one of the best months to visit. Fall at Bedner's means family outings, festive photo opportunities and plenty of seasonal fun. 'It's a day full of fun. Bring the family, cousins, aunties, grandmas it's great,' Brooker said. One of the biggest attractions is finding the perfect pumpkin. 'We have this beautiful greenery and all the pumpkins on top,' Brooker said. 'It's just a pumpkin wonderland.' Pumpkins aren't the only seasonal stars. Visitors can also spot an assortment of colorful gourds, adding even more variety to the fall display from the popping orange of the pumpkins to the golden glow of the sunflower fields. Those cheerful blooms also play an important role in the farm's ecosystem. Bedner's keeps beehives on the property, recognizing the essential role pollinators play in agriculture. entry.article_text: Fall at Bedner's means family outings, festive photo opportunities and plenty of seasonal fun."It's a day full of fun. Bring the family, cousins, aunties, grandmas — it's great," Brooker said.One of the biggest attractions is finding the perfect pumpkin."We have this beautiful greenery and all the pumpkins on top," Brooker said. "It's just a pumpkin wonderland."Pumpkins aren't the only seasonal stars. Visitors can also spot an assortment of colorful gourds, adding even more variety to the fall display — from the popping orange of the pumpkins to the golden glow of the sunflower fields.Those cheerful blooms also play an important role in the farm's ecosystem. Bedner's keeps beehives on the property, recognizing the essential role pollinators play in agriculture."We do have hives on the farm because the honeybee is the farmer's best friend," Brooker said.It's a reminder that behind the colorful fields and family-friendly attractions, there's a working farm where growing food and caring for the land go hand in hand.For a closer look at the operation, visitors can climb aboard one of the farm's tractor rides, which take you around all 80 acres of Bedner's. The ride offers more than a scenic tour. It's a glimpse into the technology and planning that keep the farm productive in South Florida's challenging climate.Tall crops help protect other plants from the wind, while drip irrigation delivers water directly where it's needed — helping keep the fields hydrated through changing weather conditions.The farm has a long agricultural history to match its modern techniques."Palm Beach County was once known as the winter produce capital of the United States," Brooker said.That legacy is still visible in the fields, where agriculture remains at the heart of the experience.Of course, no fall adventure would be complete without a corn maze — and at Bedner's, finding the exit is easier said than done. Each year brings a new maze to explore, with twists, turns and a few surprises along the way.The maze comes with its own cast of characters, including the occasional zombie and a few strategically placed scarecrows."Sometimes we have some zombie friends along the way," Brooker said.There may be a few spooky sights, but the experience is designed to be more playful than frightening. Still, the maze comes with its share of wrong turns and dead ends, but after plenty of backtracking, the exit finally comes into view.After all that walking, exploring and navigating the maze, there's only one thing left to do: cool off with a sweet treat.At Bedner's, the fall experience is about more than pumpkins and photo ops. It's about spending time outdoors, learning a little about where food comes from, and making memories with family and friends.And the best part? You can soak up all those autumn vibes without bundling up for cold weather. Because at Bedner's Farm, fall magic comes with sunshine, fresh air and just a little bit of Florida flair.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

entry.title: Local court leaders urge residents to respond to jury summonses as turnout drops
entry.summary: Court officials in Floridas 19th Judicial Circuit are warning people who ignore jury duty summonses that they could face fines and other legal consequences. The circuit serves Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. Officials say low response rates are making it harder to select juries and can delay court proceedings. At a recent WPTV Lets Hear It meetup in Okeechobee , Jerald D. Bryant, clerk of circuit court and comptroller, spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the problem. WATCH: Treasure Coast courts crack down on jury duty no-shows We just ask one thing, and we don't ask you to do it often, but people just ignore them, Bryant said. The numbers illustrate the concern. In April 2026, 300 people were summoned for jury duty, but only 60 reported. That means just one in five people showed up. Bryant said a jury summons is a court order and ignoring it can have legal consequences. It is contempt of court because a jury summons is a court order to appear, Bryant said. Why jury duty participation matters Court officials say low turnout can make it difficult to assemble a jury, potentially delaying trials and affecting defendants waiting for their cases to be heard, as well as victims and their families. Chief Judge Charles A. Schwab told WPTV that higher response rates could also help the court use its resources more efficiently. 'If we knew that return rate was going to be 75% to 85%, those other monies could then be diverted to things that we as a community would rather be spending those on,' Schwab said. What happens if you ignore a jury summons? Court leaders say they plan to enforce the consequences for people who fail to appear for jury duty. People who ignore their summonses could receive an order requiring them to explain their absence to a judge. They could face a $100 fine and still be required to serve on a jury. Failing to appear for that court hearing could lead to a bench warrant and potential arrest. Diamond Litty, public defender for the 19th judicial circuit, encouraged anyone with questions or a legitimate issue preventing them from attending to contact the court. I encourage everyone to do the right thing, to not ignore it. If you have an issue, make a phone call. There's a number on the summons, Litty said. 'Please do the right thing.' entry.summary: Early voting begins in Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast ahead of 2026 general election    WPEC
entry.article_text: Early voting begins Monday across Palm Beach County and parts of the Treasure Coast, giving voters an opportunity to cast their ballots ahead of the Nov. The start of early voting comes after a weekend of No Kings protests across South Florida, where organizers encouraged voter participation and urged residents to make a plan to vote early. The demonstrations, held Saturday in communities including West Palm Beach and Palm Beach Gardens, were part of a nationwide movement protesting President Donald Trump and his administration. This weekend’s events placed an additional focus on voter turnout ahead of the 2026 general elections. When and where can you vote early? Early voting schedules vary by county, with some polling locations opening Monday and others later in the week. There are 28 early voting locations. An additional day of early voting is available Nov. to 4 p.m., with extended hours until 6 p.m. Eligible voters can cast their ballots at any designated early voting location within the county where they are registered. Voters should bring a valid photo ID with a signature. Those without acceptable identification may still cast a provisional ballot. In Palm Beach County, voters can check polling location wait times online and use an optional appointment program to schedule their check-in time. entry.title: Ballet Palm Beach brings Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein' to the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
entry.summary: Ballet Palm Beach is bringing one of literature's most iconic stories to the stage this month with its original production of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach. The production runs Oct. 22 through Oct. 24 at the Marshall E. Rinker Sr. Playhouse and reimagines Mary Shelley's classic novel through contemporary ballet. Ballet Palm Beach describes the performance as a dramatic exploration of ambition, abandonment and identity. The company is the professional ballet company of Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast. WATCH BELOW: Ballet Palm Beach brings 'Frankenstein' to the Kravis Center Inside Ballet Palm Beach's world-premiere Frankenstein According to Founding Artistic and Executive Director Colleen Smith, the story begins before Frankenstein's monster ever comes to life. 'It's a gorgeous production about Mary Shelley and her haunting book Frankenstein,' Smith said. During the broadcast, Smith explained how the famous story was born during a gathering at Lake Geneva. 'They were gathered together on the shores of Lake Geneva on a stormy night, and Lord Byron was reading ghost stories and said, 'You know what, guys, let's create our own ghost stories,' and she did,' Smith said. 'First science fiction novel ever written by an 18-year-old woman.' Dancer Leah Walker said audiences can expect something different from a traditional ballet. 'Most classical ballets are fantasy, but ours does follow the real story of Mary Shelley and her process as she writes it,' Leah said. 'It's a horror. It's a very contemporary, very artistic take.' The production is recommended for ages 9 and older and features two 45-minute acts separated by a 20-minute intermission. For audiences looking for a Halloween-season experience with a local arts connection, the performance offers a fresh take on a familiar tale. The production combines historical elements from Mary Shelley's life with the themes that have made Frankenstein one of the most enduring stories ever written. Tickets and performance information are available through Ballet Palm Beach and the Kravis Center. entry.title: Marine life dramatically declined in Gulf years after BP oil spill, study finds
entry.summary: In a deep, dark part of the Gulf of Mexico, the number of marine animals plummeted by about 60% in the years following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon explosion, a new study found. In a crucial part of the Gulf between the light surface and the darkest depths, where the BP-operated well failed and dumped 134 million gallons of oil, the number of fish found dropped by 63.5% from the year after the spill to 2015. Crustaceans, including shrimp and krill, a key food for whales, went down 62%, and larger animals like squid and octopuses fell 59.7%, according to a study published Monday in the journal PNAS. And those populations haven't come close to recovering, the study found. Researchers focused on the ocean's 'twilight zone,' a vast area above the seafloor, where much of the surface marine life, including dolphins and whales, feast on creatures. Yet little is known about this gigantic ecosystem, and this region of the Gulf had not been studied before the 2010 spill, said study lead author Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Nova Southeastern University. A 2011 post-spill exploration cited in the research, which used six sets of nets at different depths and acoustic sonar, gave scientists a good sense of how much sea life was in the area between the surface and 5,000 feet deep. Crustaceans, including shrimp and krill, a key food for whales, went down 62%, and larger animals like squid and octopuses fell 59.7%, according to a study published Monday in the journal PNAS.And those populations haven't come close to recovering, the study found.Researchers focused on the ocean's "twilight zone," a vast area above the seafloor, where much of the surface marine life, including dolphins and whales, feast on creatures. Yet little is known about this gigantic ecosystem, and this region of the Gulf had not been studied before the 2010 spill, said study lead author Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Nova Southeastern University.A 2011 post-spill exploration cited in the research, which used six sets of nets at different depths and acoustic sonar, gave scientists a good sense of how much sea life was in the area between the surface and 5,000 feet deep. They returned to the same place with the same equipment three-and-a-half years later and found sea life was between one-third and one-quarter of what it was in 2011."We saw this big decline," Sutton said. "The question was then why? So we looked at all of the natural variables we thought could account for it, namely temperature, oxygen supply and food. None of those vary with the decline. The event that did was the oil spill. So we think that’s the most likely cause of the decline."Researchers kept on sampling since 2015 and the low populations remained, with a slight rise in 2022 and 2023 that did not prove statistically significant or lasting, Sutton said.Sutton's team documented the population declines with three different lines of evidence: what they caught in the nets, what their acoustic sonar found and genetic studies showing the species losing genetic diversity because of inbreeding.A lot of marine life died instantly after the explosion, which killed 11 workers, and from nearly five months of leaking oil and gas. Those pollutants got stored in the eggs of survivors and subsequent generations of critters got more compromised and weaker, Sutton said.BP spokesperson Paul Takahashi said the accident “forever changed” the company: “We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again.”Both the oil and the dispersants used to clean the spill hurt fish, but in different ways, said study co-author Isabel Romero, a chemical oceanographer at the University of South Carolina. Oil is more toxic and an overall threat, but the dispersant breaks the oil into smaller droplets, increasing the exposure of animals that live in the deeper water column, she said.Dispersants caused many problems, and new studies show that in future accidents, it would be better to avoid those chemicals and instead add agents that increase oil-munching microbes, said former National Science Foundation Director Rita Colwell, a University of Maryland environmental microbiologist who headed a 10-year, $500 million BP-funded program to study spill effects.Sutton said his team couldn’t prove an exact causal link to the BP oil spill, but by eliminating the other possibilities and looking at the timing, it's logically clear that the spill caused the problem.The krill population dropped 72%. Lanternfish — odd fish with blue-green lights embedded over their bodies — are a third of what they used to be, Sutton said. The stunning but scary dragonfish — with sharp teeth, light organs and a lure attached to its head — also had big losses, he said."These are foundational species," Sutton said. "They're the things most things eat. So it's no wonder that we had wholesale changes across the community."Scientists learned much about this unexplored area of the Gulf.“One of our biggest findings from the whole thing is how connected the whole oceanic Gulf is from top to bottom because the animals move up and down,” Sutton said. “There are predators at the top that dive deep. Lots of things that are deep that come up at night. So the system is one very large pulsing system, rather than just a layered system like people might have thought beforehand.”Outside scientists were especially bothered by where the spill damaged.“We know more about space in some ways than we do about the inner ocean. Because we can’t see these regions, there is a tendency to assume everything is fine, but here we have a clear result showing that something went very wrong," Scripps Institution of Oceanography marine scientist Kaitlin Frasier said in an email.Frasier, who wasn't part of the study released Monday, published a post-spill study in 2024 looking at Gulf of Mexico whales and dolphins, finding population drops as high as 83%."It's shocking how a single failure in a drilling rig can have this vast and sustained impact over thousands of square kilometers, with little visible recovery over 13 years after the spill," said Dalhousie University marine scientist Boris Worm, who wasn't part of the study. "It is important that we see this, because for the longest time these consequences were completely out of sight and out of mind."Worm and Colwell said this damage should be kept in mind as the world talks about deep-sea mining and increased oil drilling in deep waters.___The Associated Press' climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. entry.article_text: All lanes of Florida’s Turnpike have reopened in St. Lucie County after a truck fire and a separate crash caused major delays Tuesday morning. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area led to another closure. As of the latest update, all southbound lanes have reopened and traffic is beginning to move through the area. However, motorists may continue to experience residual delays as congestion clears. It’s unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WFLX has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated if more information becomes available.

entry.title: More than 120 cats, kittens found in Port St. Lucie home in alleged hoarding situation
entry.summary: WPTV is learning more about another animal hoarding situation on the Treasure Coast. Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found in a home off the 2500 block of Warwick Street. WATCH BELOW: More than 120 cats found in Port St. Lucie home 124 cats recovered from animal hoarding situation in Port St Lucie Investigators said they found the home in unsanitary conditions, including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens. Police said two of the three people living inside the home where the cats were found were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention. Sarah Wees, executive director of The Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said they were brought in 106 cats and kittens. 'They likely had to fight for food, which is why some of them are underweight, and some of the kittens that are nursing, they might be nursing on the wrong mother,' Wees said. 'If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now.' Wees said almost all of the cats had fleas and ear mites, and some with open sores needed immediate medical treatment. Now, Wees said staff and volunteers are scrambling to get them well. 'They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes,' Wees said. Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are getting better fast. 'We're seeing that in just their liveliness and eagerness to approach us and take food,' Nickelson said.  However, Wees said some of the cats and kittens are still in a dangerous situation and being treated in their sick room. 'They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation,' Wees said. 'Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time.' Wees said this situation has doubled their cat population. 'It overwhelms the staff,' Wees said. 'It overwhelms our resources.' Staff are asking for donations, volunteers and fosters during these recovery efforts. 'These little babies can't do it for themselves,' Wee said. 'So, we and the community need to do it for them.' Once medical needs are met, the cats and kittens will be up for adoption.

entry.title: Oculina Bank: Rare Florida coral reef faces pivotal federal decision over return of shrimp trawling
entry.summary: A years-long fight over one of the world's rarest ecosystems has reached federal officials, as scientists and conservationists push back against a proposal that could reopen part of the protected Oculina Bank to shrimp trawling for the first time in decades. The Oculina Bank is a deep-water coral reef off Florida's Atlantic coast, with some of its most significant formations off Fort Pierce. Built by the rare Oculina varicosa coral, the reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and provides habitat for thousands of marine species, including economically important snapper and grouper. WATCH BELOW: Fight over rare coral reef reaches NOAA as public comment opens Rare Florida reef faces federal decision on shrimp trawling Scientists say decades of shrimp trawling destroyed roughly 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place. Parts of the Oculina Bank were closed to trawling beginning in the 1990s, with protections later expanded and made permanent. Now, conservationists fear some of that progress could be reversed. 'I'd say it's dire. It's a dire situation,' said Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society. 'We're desperate to get this protected.' A push to reopen protected waters The latest battle began after a Trump administration executive order directed the nation's regional fishery councils to look for ways to reduce regulatory burdens, expand fishing opportunities and increase economic profitability. The South Atlantic Fishery Management Council subsequently considered proposals that would restore commercial shrimping access to portions of the Oculina Bank that have been protected from trawling for decades. Council documents described the areas as historically important fishing grounds and said the changes were intended to help achieve optimum yield in the rock shrimp fishery. Shrimpers say they need the additional fishing grounds. 'The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction,' Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fisheries Association, previously told WPTV. Council data reviewed by WPTV shows the rock shrimp industry has declined dramatically. The number of annual trips fell from more than 700 in the mid-1990s to fewer than 100 annually since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers also dropped from 144 in 1996 to fewer than 30 in later years. Council documents described the areas as historically important fishing grounds and said the changes were intended to help achieve optimum yield in the rock shrimp fishery.Shrimpers say they need the additional fishing grounds."The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction," Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fisheries Association, previously told WPTV.Council data reviewed by WPTV shows the rock shrimp industry has declined dramatically. The number of annual trips fell from more than 700 in the mid-1990s to fewer than 100 annually since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers also dropped from 144 in 1996 to fewer than 30 in later years.Zales has blamed the decline on factors including rising costs, imported shrimp and the loss of fishing grounds. Shrimpers have also faced increasing restrictions off Port Canaveral during space launches.Scientists and conservationists argue the potential benefit to the shrimp industry is small compared with the ecological and economic value of protecting the remaining reef.NOAA data previously reviewed by WPTV showed brown rock shrimp landings nationwide totaled about 600,000 pounds in 2023, worth roughly $1 million.Florida fishermen, by comparison, landed nearly 100 million pounds of fish worth just under $300 million that year, including species such as snapper and grouper that use the reef as habitat."We know how valuable this reef system is," Perry said.Scientists also warn that recovery from additional damage could take generations."It would take centuries to grow back even some semblance of the corals," Perry said.Supporters of reopening the area point to mapping that found no live coral, standing dead coral or coral rubble within the proposed trawling zones.But that same research warned sediment kicked up by trawling could drift into nearby living reef and smother coral. Scientists have also raised concerns that snapper and grouper could be caught as bycatch.WPTV Investigates has followed the debate as opposition grew locally and nationally.Earlier public comments to the council overwhelmingly opposed reopening the area. WPTV's review found about 120 of 150 comments opposed both proposals, while 25 supported both and five supported one proposal but not the other.A similar proposal approved by the council in 2022 ultimately failed to win federal approval, garnering thousands of opposing public comments from across the country. The latest proposal nevertheless continued moving forward.WPTV also previously reviewed financial disclosure records for members of the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council and found several disclosed financial interests tied to the fishing or seafood industries. Council officials told WPTV that conflicts of interest are governed by NOAA rules and federal law.Earlier this year, despite opposition from scientists, conservationists and members of the public, the council voted to recommend reopening as much as 24 square nautical miles to shrimp trawling — an area larger than Manhattan.The proposal has now reached the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which will decide whether to approve it.The Agency has posted the proposals to its Federal Registry, asking the public to weigh in before it votes. The fight is also drawing attention from national conservation organizations.Mike Gravitz, with the Marine Conservation Institute, said the debate comes as coral reefs worldwide already face pressure from warming waters, pollution and overfishing — and as countries around the world work toward protecting more of the planet's oceans."For gosh sakes, it's the last 10% of something that occurs nowhere else on Earth," Gravitz said.He said the United States has close to 25% of its ocean protected in an effective way, while international conservation efforts are moving in the opposite direction."It's really ironic to us that people would be talking about weakening protections for these deep-sea corals at a time when the world needs to do even more, not less," Gravitz said. "This administration is rolling back those protections, especially for the very large marine protected areas, some of which have been protected since Teddy Roosevelt was president." For Perry, the federal review represents the latest — and potentially decisive — stage of a fight that has stretched for years."They understood it, and they protected it," Perry said of previous federal protections, "but now it's being attacked again."Public comment on the proposal is open through Nov. 17 before federal officials make a final decision.Click here to submit a public comment."And we just really need to, you know, stand up and fight for it," Perry said.Multiple organizations have also launched petitions opposing the proposals.

entry.title: Palm Beach County moves forward with e-bike, scooter regulations amid safety concerns

The proposal comes as local governments across Palm Beach County continue grappling with the growing popularity of e-bikes and e-scooters, particularly among younger riders. "They've definitely popped up out of nowhere, they're pretty common to see in every side walk and every neighborhood."Others pointed to the growing number of riders in busy areas."More regulations for sure," said former teacher Pia Kresse.College student Melanie Zayas, who said e-scooters are popular on the Florida Atlantic University campus, said some limits make sense."For people getting around town that's good, but they can get a little crazy, especially when they're there's a lot of pedestrians out on the road," Zayas said.The proposal would require riders to slow down around pedestrians, something Zayas said she has experienced firsthand."So you've come close to getting hit by an e-scooter?" asked WPTV's Joel Lopez."Yes, I have and... It's, like, coming straight at me and I'm like 'hi, watch where you're going please,'" Zayas said.Kresse said the age and identification requirements could help improve accountability."As an ex-teacher I saw too many injuries. This is a big risk for a lot of kids and I want to see it get better before it gets worse," Kresse said. "I'm excited to see the ordinances actually take place."During the commission discussion, officials emphasized that the ordinance is largely driven by injury trends among young riders.Criminal Justice Commission Executive Director staff told commissioners that approximately 60% of the documented injuries involved children between ages 12 and 15, while 39% of injured adults were between 46 and 65 years old. Commissioners also debated how enforcement would work and whether younger riders could face disproportionate scrutiny."Is there concern youth will be over-policed, disproportionately stopped because they are young?" asked Bobby Powell.County staff and law enforcement officials repeatedly stressed that the focus will be education first."The intent is education and awareness," staff told commissioners. "They are not going to start writing and ticketing these kids as soon as they see it."The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said initial enforcement efforts would focus on outreach, safety campaigns and distributing helmets, particularly at schools where e-bike use is common. Officials said they secured grant funding to provide helmets and plan to launch a countywide awareness campaign directed at both children and parents."A lot of the parents don't understand that these items can be jailbroken and they can go from 20 miles an hour to 40 miles an hour," said County Commissioner Joel Flores.Flores said he routinely sees young riders weaving through traffic and riding at unsafe speeds."In my opinion this is not to jam them up. It's a way to protect them," said Flores. Some commissioners argued that e-bikes should be treated more like motorized vehicles than traditional bicycles."These are not bicycles. They're motor vehicles and they need to be treated like motor vehicles," said Gregg Weiss. Weiss also called for statewide action, saying better crash reporting and more consistent regulations are needed because current data collection remains limited.The ordinance could have impacts beyond unincorporated Palm Beach County.County staff told commissioners that many municipalities have expressed interest in adopting similar regulations and were waiting for the county to take the lead. Officials said both Wellington and the Town of Palm Beach already have ordinances on the books, with Palm Beach's rules being stricter than the county proposal. "A majority are interested. They were waiting for Palm Beach County to adopt this," staff told commissioners. entry.title: Boynton Beach Mall tenants told to leave by Jan. 15 as questions surround property's future
entry.summary: After more than four decades as a shopping destination in Palm Beach County, the future of Boynton Beach Mall is raising questions for the businesses and shoppers who have made it part of their lives. Tenants at the mall say they recently received lease termination notices from property owner Washington Prime Group, instructing them to vacate by Jan. 15, 2027. The notices come as questions swirl about a potential sale and what could happen to the property next. However, the City of Boynton Beach tells WPTV it has not been notified of a finalized sale. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: After 41 years, Boynton Beach Mall faces questions about what's next For some business owners, the uncertainty means preparing to leave a place that has been part of their livelihood for decades. For longtime shoppers, it could mean saying goodbye to a familiar community landmark. Kevin Ng has a personal connection to Boynton Beach Mall that stretches back decades. Sarku Japan, the restaurant he operates, has been at the mall since 1992. His father took over the business in 2006, and Ng assumed responsibility in 2020. After his father's death, Ng continued running the restaurant, preserving a piece of his family's legacy. While the possibility of leaving the mall was not entirely unexpected, the termination notice made the situation more concrete. 'It wasn't shocking for sure, but I knew this day was going to come,' Ng said. The notice informed Ng that his lease would be terminated on Jan. 15, 2027. 'It just said, unfortunately, your lease will be terminated Jan. 15; we just have to pack up and go,' he said. Now, Ng is trying to determine what comes next for him and the family business he has worked to maintain. 'What's next? I'm trying to figure that out right now,' he said. entry.title: Democrats fear slippage with Black voters makes Michigan Senate race feel ‘far closer than it should’
entry.summary: Abdul El-Sayed often talks about building a new and broad coalition of Michigan voters. A looming question in the states pivotal Senate race is whether he can keep the old one intact particularly with the Black voters who are pivotal to any Democratic victory. The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has spent months working to make inroads with traditional Democratic constituencies that did not support El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, in his bitter primary battle against Rep. Haley Stevens. POLITICAL ANALYSIS | Battle for the control of Congress Political analysis: Battle for the control of Congress And even though more than $280 million has been spent on television advertisements in Michigan since the 2026 midterm election cycle began, with billboards and campaign yard signs dotting the landscape alongside the fall colors, some political leaders wonder whether there is sufficient enthusiasm among Black voters for El-Sayed at this late stage. It only takes this much of Detroit to defect. It only takes this much of Flint to defect, said the Rev. Charles Williams II, pastor of the Historic King Solomon Baptist Church in Detroit, holding his fingers about an inch apart to drive home his point. If even a sliver of people dont turn out, you run into a huge challenge in trying to get your candidate over that line. Holding the Democratic coalition Michigan is crucial to Democrats hopes of the net four-seat gain the party needs on November 3 to win control of the Senate. If the party fails to retain the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, its path to a majority would grow much more difficult and would run almost exclusively through much redder states than this upper Midwestern perpetual political battleground. El-Sayed defeated Stevens in the August primary by just 1 percentage point a narrow victory fueled by his strong support among Arab American and Muslim communities, young voters and progressives in college towns. But Stevens had clear strengths, too: Black voters in and around Detroit largely aligned behind her, as did Jewish voters who have long expressed deep concerns with El-Sayed, who is Muslim and a strident critic of Israels actions in Gaza.
